newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt says giving Israel time to change tune.
newsitem.headline: Egypt says giving Israel time to change tune.

text.p: Egypt said on Sunday it was giving Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu a few more weeks to undo the damage it says he has done to Arab-Israeli relations since winning Israeli elections in May.
Foreign Minister Amr Moussa, speaking to the Egyptian government newspaper al-Ahram in New York, also listed five steps Egypt wanted to see from the new Israeli government.

The newspaper did not link the steps to a Middle East economic conference in Cairo in November, but they were similar to a list of demands the Egyptian ambassador to Israel has said Israel must meet for the conference to take place.

"We are hearing negative and damaging statements from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu," the newspaper quoted Amr Moussa as saying. "But he has a chance to put that right in the next few weeks," he added.
-- withdrawing from the West Bank town of Hebron
-- resuming negotiations with the Palestinians on the final status of the Palestinian territories
-- easing the closure of the territories
-- resuming Israeli-Syrian negotiations from the point where they stopped off

-- refraining from what he called "misusing the Lebanese track (of peace talks) by floating negative trial balloons which speak of Israeli withdrawal from south Lebanon while perpetuating its presence there".

Moussa said Syrian Foreign Minister Farouq al-Shara told a meeting of Arab ministers in Cairo this month that before Netanyahu took office, Israel had confirmed to Syria that it would withdraw completely from the Golan Heights -- Syria's main demand in the peace talks.

Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak said last week he had heard the same position straight from Israeli prime minister Yitzhak Rabin, who was assassinated last year, and that Rabin told this to the U.S. administration too.
"Now the (rightwing Israeli party) Likud wants to evade this agreement and start again, and this is very serious. We can't relate to this style of Likud's," Moussa said.

"One aspect of the problem is that Netanyahu wants to backtrack not only on what Yitzhak Rabin and (his successor) Shimon Peres agreed but also on what (previous Israeli prime minister) Yitzhak Shamir and Likud accepted," he added.
Mubarak criticised Netanyahu on Sunday, saying he was trying to make a problem out of the military manoeuvres the Egyptian armed forces have staged over the past two weeks.
He said that the manoeuvres were only a defensive training exercise and that Egypt remained committed to the peace treaty it signed with Israel in 1979.
